questions.stem: Which of these is a natural process that can change Earth's climate?
options: Cycles in Earth's orbit that shift where sunlight falls
Burning coal, oil and gas in power stations and vehicles
Clearing forests to make way for farmland and cities
Releasing hydrofluorocarbons from refrigerators
questions.explanation: Regular changes in the shape of Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis and the timing of the seasons alter how much sunlight reaches different latitudes in each season. Fossil fuel use, land clearing and refrigerant leaks are human activities.

questions.stem: Orbital cycles, often called Milankovitch cycles, include changes in the tilt of Earth's axis over about 41 000 years. How do they drive glacial and interglacial periods?
options: They move the continents, opening and closing ocean gateways each cycle
They change the composition of the atmosphere directly, removing CO₂
They change summer sunlight at high latitudes, so ice sheets grow or melt
They change the Sun's total output, heating and cooling all of Earth equally
questions.explanation: The orbital cycles barely change the total sunlight Earth receives, but they shift how much falls on high northern latitudes in summer. Weak summers let snow survive and ice sheets grow; strong summers melt them. Feedbacks from albedo and greenhouse gases then amplify the change.

questions.stem: Over tens to hundreds of millions of years, continents assemble into supercontinents and break apart again. How can this plate tectonic super-cycle change climate?
options: It changes the Sun's distance from Earth by moving the continents
It produces greenhouse gases only when continents collide head-on
It alters ocean currents, volcanic gas output and weathering rates
It changes the length of the day, and so daily heating, every few years
questions.explanation: Moving continents open and close seaways, redirecting ocean heat transport, while changes in volcanic activity alter the CO₂ released and mountain building changes how fast weathering removes CO₂. These act over millions of years. Plate motion does not affect the Earth-Sun distance.

questions.stem: Climate changes are evident at different time scales. Which pairing of driver and time scale is correct?
options: Human greenhouse emissions: millions of years
Tectonic super-cycle: hundreds of millions of years
Orbital cycles: a few years each, repeating often
El Niño and La Niña: tens of thousands of years
questions.explanation: The super-cycle of continents assembling and breaking up takes hundreds of millions of years. Orbital cycles run over tens of thousands of years, El Niño and La Niña over months to years, and human emissions have changed the atmosphere over about two centuries.

questions.stem: Changes in ocean circulation can change regional climate within decades. Which mechanism illustrates this?
options: Ocean currents create new greenhouse gases as they flow past the poles
A weaker ocean conveyor carries less heat to high latitudes, cooling them
A stronger ocean conveyor stops evaporation, so rainfall falls everywhere
Ocean currents change the tilt of Earth's axis by shifting water mass
questions.explanation: The ocean conveyor moves enormous amounts of heat poleward. If it weakened, regions that depend on that heat, such as north-west Europe, would cool even as the planet warms on average. Ocean circulation redistributes energy; it does not change Earth's tilt.

questions.stem: Which human activities are the main sources of the extra carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: Burning fossil fuels and clearing land
Growing rice and raising cattle herds
Using nitrogen fertilisers on crops
Leaking refrigerants from old fridges
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon stored for millions of years, and clearing and burning vegetation releases carbon stored in biomass and soils. Rice paddies and cattle are major methane sources, fertilisers release nitrous oxide, and refrigerants include hydrofluorocarbons.

questions.stem: Which gas comes mainly from nitrogen fertilisers used in agriculture?
options: Nitrous oxide
Methane
Ozone
Hydrofluorocarbons
questions.explanation: Soil microbes convert part of the nitrogen in fertilisers into nitrous oxide, a long-lived greenhouse gas. Methane comes mostly from livestock, rice, landfill and fossil fuel production, and hydrofluorocarbons are manufactured chemicals.

questions.stem: What makes hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) different from the other main greenhouse gases that humans emit?
options: They are entirely manufactured, with no natural source
They are released only by volcanoes and never by people
They absorb no infrared radiation at all
They are removed from the air within a few hours
questions.explanation: HFCs are synthetic gases made for refrigeration and air conditioning, so all of them in the atmosphere come from human activity. Many trap far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide also have natural sources.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: Cooling caused by ozone loss over Antarctica each spring
Warming caused by a long-term rise in the Sun's output
Extra warming as human emissions add greenhouse gases
The natural warming that keeps Earth's water mostly liquid
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases occur naturally and keep Earth habitable. When human activities add more of them, more outgoing infrared is returned to the surface, causing additional warming: the enhanced greenhouse effect. Solar output has not risen to match recent warming.

questions.stem: Burning fossil fuels releases sulfate aerosols as well as carbon dioxide. Why do scientists say aerosols have partly masked the warming from greenhouse gases?
options: Sulfate aerosols reflect sunlight, cooling the surface
Sulfate aerosols absorb carbon dioxide, removing it from the air
Sulfate aerosols are greenhouse gases that trap even more heat
Sulfate aerosols thicken the ozone layer, blocking infrared radiation
questions.explanation: Sulfate particles scatter incoming sunlight back to space and help form brighter clouds, which cools the surface. They wash out within days to weeks, while carbon dioxide persists for centuries, so cutting aerosol pollution can uncover extra warming. Some particles, such as soot, warm instead.

questions.stem: How does clearing native forest for farmland change the composition of the atmosphere?
options: Stored carbon is released as CO₂, and less CO₂ is taken up
Oxygen levels rise, because grasslands release more oxygen than forests
Water vapour is removed, so the greenhouse effect weakens permanently
Nitrogen levels fall, because trees are the main source of nitrogen gas
questions.explanation: Burning or decay of cleared vegetation releases its stored carbon, and the replacement crops or pasture store far less, so carbon dioxide rises. Clearing also changes albedo and local water cycling. Nitrogen and oxygen levels are not noticeably changed.

questions.stem: Antarctic ice cores show carbon dioxide between about 180 and 280 ppm over the past 800 000 years. Direct measurements now show more than 400 ppm. What do these data together indicate?
options: CO₂ levels always rise to 400 ppm at the end of each glacial period
Ice cores cannot record CO₂, so no comparison can be made
Present CO₂ is far above the range of the past 800 000 years
Present CO₂ is within the natural range seen in glacial cycles
questions.explanation: Air trapped in the ice shows that CO₂ rose and fell between about 180 and 280 ppm through glacial cycles. Values above 400 ppm are far outside that range, and the rise has happened in about two centuries, matching fossil fuel use and land clearing.

questions.stem: Which of these is a greenhouse gas released mainly by livestock digestion, rice paddies and landfill?
options: Methane
Nitrous oxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Microbes that break down organic matter without oxygen, in cattle and sheep stomachs, flooded rice fields and landfill, produce methane. Nitrous oxide comes mainly from fertilised soils. Oxygen and nitrogen are not significant greenhouse gases.

questions.stem: An ice core shows temperature and carbon dioxide rising together at the end of a glacial period, with the temperature rise starting slightly earlier in some records. How do scientists interpret this?
options: Temperature and CO₂ are unrelated, and the match is a coincidence
Orbital changes began the warming, and rising CO₂ then amplified it
Carbon dioxide cannot affect temperature, because it rose second
The ice core dating must be wrong, because CO₂ always rises first
questions.explanation: At glacial terminations, orbital changes started the warming; warmer oceans then released carbon dioxide, which trapped more heat and amplified the warming. CO₂ acts as both a feedback and a driver. Today it is rising first, because humans are adding it directly.

questions.stem: Which two processes contribute most to global sea level rise as the climate warms?
options: Melting of floating sea ice and increased rainfall
Sinking of the sea floor and more river sediment
Increased evaporation and more frequent cyclones
Thermal expansion of seawater and melting land ice
questions.explanation: Warmer water expands, and melting glaciers and ice sheets on land add water to the oceans. Floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water, so its melting barely changes sea level.

questions.stem: Over recent decades, many species have been recorded further south in Australia, or higher up mountains, than before. How does this link to climate change?
options: Species are following cooler conditions as their ranges warm
Species are moving towards warmer areas to escape colder winters
Species are moving because the continents have shifted position
Species are moving because sea level has fallen along the coast
questions.explanation: As temperatures rise, the conditions a species tolerates shift towards the poles and to higher altitudes, and many species follow. Species that cannot move, such as those already on mountain tops, may lose their habitat. Continental drift is far too slow to matter.

questions.stem: Climate change affects the biosphere, atmosphere, geosphere and hydrosphere. Which example shows an effect on the hydrosphere?
options: Shifts in the ranges of native birds and insects inland
Faster weathering of exposed rock surfaces
Changes in the flowering times of crops
Shrinking ice sheets and changed rainfall patterns
questions.explanation: The hydrosphere includes oceans, rivers, rain, groundwater and ice, so shrinking ice sheets and changes in rainfall are hydrosphere effects. Species ranges and flowering times are biosphere effects, and weathering of rock affects the geosphere.

questions.stem: Rainfall in the south-west of Western Australia has declined since about 1970, and inflows to Perth's dams have fallen even more sharply. Why do the inflows fall by a larger proportion than the rainfall?
options: Drier soils soak up more of each rain, so less runs off
The dams leak more water to the sea as the climate warms
Lower rainfall raises the water table, so rivers flow inland
Less rainfall means more water vapour, which fills the dams
questions.explanation: When rain falls on dry soil, much of it soaks in or evaporates before it can run off. A modest drop in rainfall therefore causes a much larger drop in runoff and streamflow. This shows how a change in the atmosphere cascades through the hydrosphere and geosphere.

questions.stem: How might warmer temperatures and changed rainfall affect crop productivity in Australia?
options: Crop productivity cannot change, because farmers control all conditions
All crops will fail at once once temperatures rise by any amount
Effects vary: some regions lose yield to heat and drought; some gain
All crops everywhere will grow faster because of the extra carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Heat waves and drought reduce yields in many cropping areas, while longer growing seasons may help some cooler regions. Extra CO₂ can boost growth of some crops, but not enough to offset heat and water stress everywhere. The effects differ by region and crop.

questions.stem: Warmer ocean temperatures have caused repeated mass bleaching of corals on the Great Barrier Reef. What happens during coral bleaching?
options: Corals freeze in cold water, killing the algae that give them colour
Heat-stressed corals expel the algae in their tissues, losing colour and food
Corals absorb extra sunlight and turn white as their limestone skeletons grow faster
Corals are buried by sediment from rivers, which bleaches their surfaces
questions.explanation: Reef-building corals depend on algae in their tissues for much of their food. Prolonged heat stress makes corals expel the algae, so they turn white and starve; many die if the heat lasts. This is a direct biosphere effect of a warming hydrosphere.

questions.stem: How do ice cores provide evidence of past atmospheric composition?
options: Bubbles sealed in as snow turned to ice preserve ancient air
Layers of ice record the exact temperature on each day in the past
Fossils of animals frozen in the ice show which gases they breathed
The colour of the ice shows how much carbon dioxide was in the air
questions.explanation: As snow builds up and compacts into ice, small bubbles of air are sealed in. Analysing that air gives past concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane. Annual layers help date the ice, and isotopes in the ice itself indicate past temperature.

questions.stem: Pollen grains preserved in layers of lake sediment can be identified to plant type. How do they show past climate change?
options: The number of pollen grains shows how much carbon dioxide was in the air
Pollen grains grow larger in warm years, giving yearly temperatures
Pollen grains contain ice crystals that record the air temperature
Changes in the plants present show how temperature and rainfall changed
questions.explanation: Each plant type grows within certain temperature and rainfall ranges. A shift down a sediment core from, say, rainforest pollen to grass and eucalypt pollen shows the climate became drier. The layers are dated, giving a timeline of change.

questions.stem: In shells of marine microfossils (foraminifera), a higher ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 is found in layers from glacial periods. Why?
options: Glacial seas contained more oxygen gas, so all oxygen isotopes increased
Oxygen-18 forms from oxygen-16 when seawater freezes into sea ice
Warm water contains more oxygen-18, so glacial shells formed in warm seas
Ice sheets stored lighter oxygen-16, leaving seawater richer in oxygen-18
questions.explanation: Water containing lighter oxygen-16 evaporates more easily, and in glacial periods that water fell as snow and was stored in ice sheets. The oceans were left enriched in oxygen-18, which the shells recorded. Isotopic ratios therefore track ice volume and temperature.

questions.stem: Fossils of tropical plants and coal formed from swamp forests are found in rocks in Antarctica. What can be concluded?
options: Tropical plants can grow under thick ice sheets in very cold climates
The fossils were carried to Antarctica by glaciers from the tropics
Antarctica's climate has stayed the same since the plants first grew
The area was once much warmer, partly because the continent was elsewhere
questions.explanation: The fossils show a warm, wet environment once existed there. Over hundreds of millions of years, both global climate and the continent's position changed, so fossils record climate change over geological time. Glaciers erode and deposit debris; they do not transport whole fossil forests.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a historical (rather than geological) record of climate?
options: Layers of glacial deposits in very old rocks
Daily temperature readings kept since the 1800s
Oxygen isotopes in deep-sea sediment cores
Fossil leaves preserved in ancient lake beds
questions.explanation: Historical records come from people: instrument readings, logbooks, diaries and photographs over the past few centuries. Isotopes in sediment cores, fossil leaves and glacial deposits are geological records covering much longer periods.

questions.stem: Records show that, after the last glacial period, some regions warmed quickly while others changed little, and some species expanded while others retreated. What does this show?
options: Climate change has the same effect everywhere, so local records are wrong
Only species, not regions, are affected by changes in climate
Regional differences prove that the glacial period did not happen
Climate change affects different regions and species in different ways
questions.explanation: Past records show that the same global change produced different local effects, depending on latitude, ocean currents, landscape and how each species responds. That is why records from many places and types of evidence are combined.

questions.stem: Scientists compare several kinds of evidence, such as ice cores, pollen and ocean isotopes, when reconstructing past climate. Why?
options: Only one kind of record can be dated, so the others are not reliable
Using more records makes the past climate warmer in the reconstruction
Independent records that agree give stronger evidence than one
Each record measures exactly the same thing, so they can be averaged
questions.explanation: Each proxy has its own limitations, dating method and region. When independent records from different places and methods show the same pattern, confidence in the reconstruction is much higher. They measure different things, such as vegetation, gas concentrations or ice volume.

questions.stem: What is a general circulation model (GCM) in climate science?
options: A physical scale model of Earth placed in a wind tunnel to study air flow
A map showing the paths of ocean currents and winds at one moment
A list of past temperatures used to forecast the next season's weather
A computer model of the atmosphere and oceans as grid cells obeying physical laws
questions.explanation: GCMs split the atmosphere, oceans, land and ice into a three-dimensional grid and use the equations of energy, mass and motion to calculate how each cell changes over time. They simulate how the oceans and atmosphere behave and interact.

questions.stem: How do scientists test whether a climate model is reliable before using it to project the future?
options: They test it by predicting the exact weather on a chosen future day
They run it for past periods and compare it with observed climate
They check that it gives the same result as last year's weather forecast
They run it once and accept the result if it shows any warming
questions.explanation: Models are built from past and current climate data, and tested by 'hindcasting': simulating past climate, such as the twentieth century or the last glacial period, and comparing with records. Climate models project long-term averages, not daily weather.

questions.stem: Climate models are used to predict the response of global climate to changes in its components. Which is an example of such a component change?
options: A reduction in global ice cover lowering Earth's albedo
A single severe storm crossing the coastline next week
A change in the price of electricity in one country
A new satellite being launched to observe the weather
questions.explanation: Models explore how climate responds to changes such as atmospheric composition and ice cover. Losing ice lowers albedo, so more sunlight is absorbed, a feedback models must include. Individual storms are weather, and prices and satellites are not climate components.

questions.stem: Different climate models agree closely on global average warming for a given rise in greenhouse gases, but disagree more about rainfall changes in particular regions. Why?
options: Global temperature is measured directly in the models, but rainfall is guessed
Rainfall is not affected by climate change, so models simply contradict each other
Global averages are calculated with less physics than regional rainfall is
Rainfall depends on small processes, such as clouds, that models only approximate
questions.explanation: Clouds and storms are smaller than a model's grid cells, so they must be approximated, and rainfall depends strongly on them and on local landscape. Global temperature reflects the overall energy balance, which models capture well. This shows the limits of models as well as their uses.

questions.stem: Models of El Niño and La Niña couple the ocean and atmosphere. Why must both be included?
options: The atmosphere alone controls sea temperatures over the Pacific
Only the ocean floor's shape matters for these events
Winds change sea temperatures, which in turn change the winds
The ocean alone controls the winds, so the atmosphere can be ignored
questions.explanation: In El Niño and La Niña, trade winds move warm surface water, and the pattern of sea temperatures changes air pressure and the winds, which feed back on the ocean. A model of only one sphere cannot reproduce this interaction or forecast the events months ahead.

questions.stem: Why are climate models built using large amounts of past and present climate data?
options: The data replace the need for any physical laws inside the models
The data show the exact weather on every day for the next century
The data are needed only to make the models run faster on computers
The data show how the climate behaves, so models can be built and checked
questions.explanation: Observations of temperature, rainfall, ocean heat, ice and gases reveal how the climate system works and provide a test for model results. The models still rely on physical laws; data constrain and check them. Models project trends, not daily weather.

questions.stem: A model run with only natural drivers (solar and volcanic changes) fails to reproduce the global warming observed since about 1950, but a run that also includes human emissions matches it well. What does this suggest?
options: Human emissions are needed to explain recent warming
Natural drivers alone fully explain recent warming
The observations must be wrong, as natural drivers dominate
Models cannot say anything useful about causes of warming
questions.explanation: Comparing model runs with and without human emissions is one way scientists attribute causes. Only the runs including greenhouse gases and aerosols reproduce the observed warming, so natural drivers alone cannot explain it. This is evidence, combined with other lines of evidence, about the cause.

questions.stem: Why do climate projections usually give a range of possible outcomes rather than a single number?
options: A range is used only to make the results easier to read
Future emissions and some physical processes are uncertain
The models give random answers, so any value is equally likely
Scientists cannot calculate temperatures, only guess them
questions.explanation: Projections depend on how much greenhouse gas people emit, which is uncertain, and on processes such as cloud feedbacks that differ between models. Running many scenarios and models gives a range. The results are not random; they are constrained by physics and data.
